case_study_insert.main_stem: Orchard Valley Juice (OVJ) is a public limited company in the soft-drinks industry, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2005 by Nadia Orchard, the business sells cold-pressed juice to national supermarkets and health shops and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. OVJ plans to invest $720,000 in a new cold-press bottling line to expand capacity, financed by a $420,000 share issue and a $300,000 bank loan. It has fixed costs of $280,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $12.50, and produces 90,000 units a year. OVJ faces two problems: labour turnover is rising and fruit waste has reached 5.8% of throughput.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Market Report - Q3 2025: OVJ bottled 21,400 units of juice last quarter at a defect rate of 2.1%, down from 3.5% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 52 to 29 a month. Fruit waste reached 5.8% of throughput. Average delivery time is 3.1 days. A survey of 700 shoppers found 66% would pay up to $0.60 more for cold-pressed juice, and 49% check added-sugar labels. A training review shows 22 of 55 operators need certification on the new bottling line; courses cost $840 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Orchard Valley Juice as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.50% to 5.25%, raising interest costs on OVJ's $300,000 variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.9% from $12.90 to $13.79 an hour from April 2026. (3) Fruit input prices have risen 13.1% year-on-year, soft-drink inflation is 7.9% and consumer spending on healthy drinks grew 5.2%.

questions.question_text: OVJ has raised $420,000 through a share issue and $300,000 through a bank loan. Explain two advantages for OVJ of the share issue over the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Share issue money does not have to be repaid and carries no mandatory interest, so the $420,000 reduces the debt burden while OVJ funds a $720,000 bottling line and services only the $300,000 loan. With fixed costs of $280,000 a year and fruit waste at 5.8%, keeping cash free matters more than diluting ownership, and the $12.50 selling price need not cover extra interest.

Point 2: A public limited company can raise a large sum from many investors, so the $420,000 is available in one step rather than being limited by retained profit or bank lending limits. New shareholders also bring no fixed repayment date, which suits a long-life bottling asset, and the share issue can be used alongside the 66% of 700 shoppers who would pay $0.60 more for cold-pressed juice to expand capacity. Democratic leadership can involve shareholders in long-term goals, supporting the 90,000-unit plan, and the extra equity directly improves planning.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: OVJ is launching a new no-added-sugar juice. Consider supermarket shelf promotions, influencer marketing, or sponsorship of a food festival. Which should OVJ choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Supermarket shelf promotions: Shelf displays put the new juice directly beside shoppers at the national supermarkets that already stock OVJ, and can highlight the 49% who check added-sugar labels. They are cheap and measurable through the 21,400 units sold last quarter. The weakness is competition for prime shelf space and retailer fees, which could squeeze the $7.00 contribution needed to justify the $720,000 line, and a display does not explain cold-press benefits.

Influencer marketing: Health and lifestyle influencers can reach exactly the shoppers who value cold-pressed juice, with the 66% of 700 buyers willing to pay $0.60 more targeted at low cost per contact. Content can show the added-sugar label clearly and is measurable. The drawbacks are slow trust-building, dependence on influencer credibility, and limited in-store conversion; with labour turnover rising in a workforce of 55, OVJ may lack staff to manage many campaigns.

Food festival sponsorship: Sponsorship gives large-scale tasting and brand visibility, letting consumers try the product and ask questions, which fits a 3.1-day delivery lead time and national ambitions. It is expensive, however, and attendees may not be regular supermarket buyers; the 5.8% fruit waste means samples must be carefully planned, and reach is concentrated in a few events.

Recommendation: OVJ should choose influencer marketing. It targets the 66% premium segment and the 49% checking labels at low cost, and can be measured before scaling, which suits a publicly listed firm with a $300,000 loan to protect. Shelf promotions are rejected because retailer fees and space competition limit margin; festival sponsorship is rejected as costly and narrow compared with year-round digital reach. OVJ can add shelf cards once awareness is built.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to OVJ.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses at least two options with advantages and disadvantages applied to OVJ.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of OVJ with a justified recommendation and clear rejection of the alternatives.

questions.question_text: OVJ's labour turnover is rising and fruit waste has reached 5.8%. Explain two benefits for OVJ of using team working on its bottling line.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Organising the 55 staff into teams around the new bottling line gives operators shared responsibility for output and quality, breaking repetitive work and reducing the labour turnover that disrupts the 21,400 units bottled last quarter. Teams can spot the causes of the 5.8% fruit waste together, protecting the $12.50 price and the $7.00 contribution per unit.

Point 2: Team working spreads skills, so the 22 of 55 operators needing certification can learn from colleagues while only a smaller number take the $840 courses, saving cost on top of the $720,000 investment. Under democratic leadership, team suggestions are heard through the hierarchy, improving the 2.1% defect rate and helping the 90,000-unit target. Stronger team commitment also reduces absence-related disruption to the 3.1-day delivery time demanded by national supermarkets, which helps the 49% of shoppers checking added-sugar labels receive consistent juice. It also raises morale, reducing the labour turnover that currently disrupts production.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: OVJ needs a technician for the new bottling line. Consider training an existing operator or appointing a qualified technician from outside. Which should OVJ choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Training an existing operator: An internal trainee already knows OVJ's bottling routine and quality standards, so training is faster to apply and keeps loyalty in a workforce of 55 where labour turnover is rising. It avoids external recruitment fees and uses the $840 course budget for the 22 of 55 operators needing certification, supporting democratic leadership and cutting the 2.1% defect rate. The drawback is that training takes time, and the 5.8% fruit waste may persist until the trainee is competent on the new $720,000 line.

Appointing a qualified technician from outside: An experienced outside technician brings proven skills and can cut the 2.1% defect rate and 5.8% waste immediately, useful for a public limited company answerable to shareholders. Fresh expertise helps maintain the 90,000-unit target and 3.1-day delivery time. However, recruitment and salary costs are higher on top of a $300,000 loan, and an outsider may be resented by the 22 of 55 staff still awaiting certification, worsening turnover.

Decision: OVJ should train an existing operator, with a short external course where needed. Internal training is cheaper, builds commitment and directly addresses the rising turnover using the $840 budget, while preserving knowledge of the 90,000-unit process. An outside appointment is rejected because the added salary cost and resentment outweigh the speed gain while a $300,000 loan is serviced; OVJ can hire a specialist later if the 2.1% defect rate does not fall, once the internal trainee is certified and the $720,000 line is stable. This also keeps the 3.1-day delivery promise reliable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two staffing choices with limited application to OVJ.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both choices in the context of OVJ.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both choices in the context of OVJ with a well-justified decision covering cost, skills and turnover.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how OVJ's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs / Contribution per unit. Substitution: $280,000 / ($12.50 - $5.50) = $280,000 / $7.00 = 40,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 40,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price - Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.50 - $5.50 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways OVJ's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 40,000-unit break-even output with 90,000 units actual output, giving a margin of safety of 50,000 units, to decide whether to run the new bottling line at full capacity.
2. Use $7.00 contribution to test the $0.60 premium: if won, contribution becomes $7.60 ($7.00 + $0.60), showing room to absorb retailer discounts without losing profit.
3. Combine $280,000 fixed costs with $7.00 contribution to set the volume needed to service the $300,000 loan before reporting to shareholders on the $720,000 project.
4. Unit cost of $8.61 ($280,000 / 90,000 + $5.50) can be tracked to detect the 5.8% fruit waste and 2.1% defect rate, protecting the $12.50 price.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 40,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 50,000-unit margin of safety; testing the $0.60 premium; loan-service volume targets; unit-cost benchmarking at $8.61.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate OVJ's liquidity by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has OVJ's liquidity improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.30 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.29 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.72 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.71 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $145,000 inventories + $118,000 trade receivables + $62,000 cash = $325,000; 2025 current assets = $162,000 + $150,000 + $48,000 = $360,000. Cover of the 2024 current liabilities of $250,000 was $325,000 / $250,000 = 1.30; cover of the 2025 liabilities of $278,000 was $360,000 / $278,000 = 1.29. Liquid assets excluding inventories were $325,000 - $145,000 = $180,000 in 2024, giving $180,000 / $250,000 = 0.72, and $360,000 - $162,000 = $198,000 in 2025, giving $198,000 / $278,000 = 0.71.

Evaluation: Liquidity has slightly deteriorated. Cover fell from 1.30 to 1.29 because current liabilities rose from $250,000 to $278,000 faster than current assets, which grew from $325,000 to $360,000. The liquid-asset measure fell from 0.72 to 0.71: although receivables rose from $118,000 to $150,000, cash dropped from $62,000 to $48,000 and inventories grew from $145,000 to $162,000. More of the cover now sits in stock and receivables, which is risky with 5.8% fruit waste and a 2.1% defect rate. Servicing a $300,000 loan while a $720,000 bottling line is commissioned leaves little spare cash if national supermarkets delay payment.

Conclusion: OVJ's liquidity has not improved. Both cover measures slipped and the fall in cash is the clearest warning, since the higher receivables tie up funds rather than strengthening solvency. OVJ should collect receivables faster and slow inventory growth before further borrowing.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of the current-asset components and a justified conclusion.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for OVJ of introducing a recycling scheme for its fruit waste.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycling the 5.8% fruit waste into by-products or compost reduces disposal cost and supports the 66% of 700 shoppers who would pay $0.60 more for cold-pressed juice with a sustainability story. It also cuts the 2.1% defect rate by giving rejected fruit a use, protecting the $7.00 contribution and the $12.50 selling price while the $720,000 bottling line raises throughput to 90,000 units.

Disadvantage: A recycling scheme needs extra equipment and staff time in a workforce of 55 where labour turnover is rising, and it does not stop waste occurring at source. With fixed costs of $280,000 and a $300,000 loan, the set-up cost could squeeze margins unless the $0.60 premium is fully accepted. The 49% of shoppers checking added-sugar labels care more about ingredients than waste, so the scheme may add cost without raising sales, and the 13.1% fruit price rise still raises the $5.50 variable cost. Running the scheme while commissioning the $720,000 line could also distract the 22 of 55 operators needing certification, putting the 90,000-unit target at risk.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to the named business and the case data.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 6.9% minimum wage increase and the 13.1% rise in fruit input prices will affect OVJ. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.50% to 5.25%): The change is 0.75 percentage points. If OVJ's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra annual interest is 0.75% x $300,000 = $2,250, modest beside fixed costs of $280,000 and a $720,000 expansion. A fixed-rate loan would mean no immediate extra cost. Higher rates may also cool consumer spending, but the direct figure is small and can be capped by refinancing.

Minimum wage increase (6.9%, to $13.79): OVJ has a workforce of 55, but the insert gives no hours worked or individual wages, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. Productivity is 90,000 units / 55 staff = about 1,636 units per worker. If that is maintained, the rise can be absorbed within the $5.50 variable cost and $7.00 contribution; if labour turnover and 5.8% waste reduce output, unit labour cost rises. It is a permanent rise but cannot be quantified from the insert.

Input price inflation (13.1% fruit): The insert does not break down the $5.50 variable cost, so only a labelled upper bound is sound: if all of the $5.50 rose 13.1%, that is 13.1% x $5.50 = about $0.72 per unit, or around $65,000 a year at 90,000 units. That directly erodes the $7.00 contribution servicing the $300,000 loan. OVJ can recover part through the $0.60 premium accepted by 66% of buyers, helped by the 5.2% growth in healthy-drink spending.

Conclusion: The 13.1% fruit input price rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs across all 90,000 units and attacks the contribution that funds the new line, dwarfing the $2,250 interest effect; the wage rise is also significant but unquantifiable and partly offset by productivity, whereas fruit inflation directly and repeatedly cuts the margin.
